domains.name: History, Foundations, and Philosophy of AI
domains.summary: What 'AI' has actually meant in each era, why paradigms rose and collapsed, and which conceptual arguments (Turing's, Searle's, Dreyfus's, Harnad's) still constrain how we build and evaluate systems. Teaches readers to date a claim, identify the paradigm behind it, and resist founder mythology.

subdomains.name: AI Intellectual History
subdomains.summary: Era-by-era reconstruction of the field's dominant objects of study - automata, cybernetic feedback, symbols, heuristics, probability, learned representations - and the material reasons each lost credibility and funding.

topics.name: The Successive Paradigms of AI
topics.definition: AI is best understood not as one field but as a sequence of paradigms, each defined by what it took to be the basic unit of intelligence: finite automata, feedback-regulated machines, physical symbols, domain-specific heuristics, probability distributions over hypotheses, learned hierarchical features, and now general-purpose pretrained models.
topics.explanation: The pre-history is three separate streams that later fused: Turing's 1936 computability result and his 1950 imitation game, Wiener's 1948 cybernetics with its feedback and servomechanism vocabulary, and the McCulloch-Pitts 1943 logical neuron. The 1956 Dartmouth workshop, organised by McCarthy, Minsky, Rochester and Shannon, named the field and committed it to the claim that every aspect of learning could in principle be simulated by a machine operating on symbol structures. The GOFAI era (roughly 1957-1980) produced ITS, GPS, the Logic Theorist and later SHRDLU, all treating intelligent behaviour as symbolic manipulation guided by heuristics. The expert-systems boom (1980-1993) commercialised that stance as knowledge engineering, then collapsed when maintenance costs and brittleness exceeded the value delivered. Two revivals followed in parallel: connectionism, re-launched by Rumelhart-Hinton-Williams 1986 backpropagation and the PDP volumes, and the statistical turn, in which probability and later learning theory replaced hand-written rules as the object of study, marked by the 1994 AAAI switch to machine-learning tracks. Deep learning (2012 onward) and foundation models (2018 onward) are the third and fourth statistical-era shifts: scale plus gradient descent plus web data, with representations, not rules, as the primary artefact. Each transition changed what counted as an explanation: from 'the program searches a space of problem states', to 'the rule base encodes an expert's heuristic', to 'the model maximises likelihood over a hypothesis class', to 'the model exhibits capabilities that emerge with scale'. The transitions were not purely intellectual - each was funded by a different patron (DARPA, the Japanese Fifth Generation project, corporate AI labs, web companies) and each patron's interests shaped what counted as progress.
learning_objectives: Date a quoted AI claim to an era and name the paradigm that makes the claim natural.
Contrast GOFAI, expert-system, statistical, deep-learning and foundation-model conceptions of what an AI system is.
Explain why cybernetics and connectionism are not ancestors of the same thing - one studied closed-loop control, the other studied representation learning.
Identify the material (funding and compute) conditions behind at least two paradigm shifts.
State what counts as an explanation in each paradigm and why cross-paradigm debates often talk past each other.

Understanding why rule-based and learned approaches coexist in production systems
common_misconceptions: 'AI' is one continuous discipline interrupted by two winters - in reality the disciplines, mathematics, institutions and even the word's referent changed repeatedly.

Cybernetics failed because it was wrong; it failed largely because its universalist claims outran the available computation and because it dissolved into control engineering, robotics and AI rather than being refuted.
Connectionism 'won' over symbolism; most working systems today are hybrids, and the symbolic legacy is embedded in type systems, planning languages, ontologies and program synthesis.

topics.name: AI Winters: Overpromise, Patron Withdrawal, and the Cycle
topics.definition: An AI winter is a period in which funding, hiring and credibility contract sharply after a phase of public overpromise; the two canonical cases are the mid-1970s and the early 1990s, and both were driven as much by the withdrawal of a specific patron as by scientific failure.
topics.explanation: The first winter followed the Lighthill report (1973), commissioned by the UK Science Research Council to assess AI. Sir James Lighthill's verdict was not that machines could never be intelligent but that AI had failed to deliver on the grand claims of the 1965 Royal Seminar and had made problems involving combinatorial search harder than it admitted; his recommended remedy - narrow, useful work such as pattern recognition - was taken by departments as a death sentence, and British AI funding collapsed. The second winter had several independent causes that reinforced each other: expert systems required continuous, expensive, bespoke maintenance (the 'knowledge-engineering bottleneck' Hayes-Roth documented), Lisp machines lost a market contest to general-purpose hardware and C, and connectionism's early successes did not translate into products fast enough. DARPA's shift away from long-horizon autonomous reasoning programmes, and the Japanese Fifth Generation project's failure to produce a marketable Prolog machine, closed the last large state patronage channel. The recurring mechanism is a promise-expectation-funding loop: a headline capability claim attracts money, the claim is not met on schedule, and the whole field - including work that was quietly succeeding - loses resources. The 1990s response was a deliberate, and mostly successful, discipline: the field adopted statistical method and measurable benchmarks partly because they were defensible to sceptical patrons. Current practice of reporting capability without stating deployment horizons is the same lesson in a new form. The honest diagnosis is that neither winter involved a refutation of AI's core possibilities; both were corrections in claimed timelines, compounded by the concentration of funding in a small number of non-scientific decision-makers.

common_misconceptions: 'The winters proved scaling symbolic AI was impossible' - they proved it could not meet announced deadlines at announced cost.
Winter is a scientific phenomenon; the two canonical winters were overwhelmingly funding and market events with scientific content only secondarily.
Today's field is immune because funding is private and abundant - private concentration creates different but real fragilities.

subdomains.name: Philosophy of Machine Intelligence and Cognition
subdomains.summary: The arguments about what a machine could understand, whether behaviour suffices for mind, and how human cognition constrains or fails to constrain artificial systems.

topics.name: The Imitation Game, Its Critiques, and Modern Evaluation
topics.definition: Turing's 1950 proposal replaces the unanswerable question 'can machines think?' with an operational one: would an unwilling human interrogator, judging only by conversation, be systematically unable to tell machine from human? It is an evaluation protocol and a philosophical move at once, and both have been contested in specific, learnable ways.
topics.explanation: Turing's paper did several things at once: it disposed of 'thinking' as a definitional problem, anticipated learning rather than programming as the route to capability, and listed nine objections to machine intelligence (the theological, 'heads of the Irish school', mathematical, consciousness, other-disabilities, Lady Lovelace, informality, ESP and clairsentience objections) with replies that remain the standard taxonomy. The strongest mathematical objection is not Gödelian - Turing's own response was that a machine can be wrong, whereas a mathematician asserting a theorem presumably is right - but rather that no behavioural test can establish the presence of understanding. Searle's 1980 Chinese Room makes that case: executing a program that manipulates Chinese symbols correctly is, he argues, exactly what the room's occupant does while understanding nothing, so symbol manipulation plus correct output is not sufficient for intentionality. The replies are standard and worth knowing: the systems reply (understanding belongs to the whole system, not the man), the robot reply (ground the symbols in perception and action), the brain-substitute reply, and the behavioural/conventionalist reply that 'understanding' is not a further fact beyond disposition. French's review of fifty years of the test emphasises the practical point: the test as posed is not a good engineering target, because unmodified chat success is achievable with retrieval, deception and topic dodging, and because interrogators are easily biased by style cues. Modern capability evaluation inherited this problem: benchmarks are behavioural, are gameable by memorisation and prompt tuning, and conflate the ability to produce a form with the ability to verify it. The defensible position is that the imitation game is a useful thought experiment about the sufficiency of behaviour and a poor experimental protocol, and that 'passing' has always been ambiguous until you specify what the judge is permitted to see.

Reconstruct Turing's nine objections and his replies in his own terms, including his response to the mathematical objection.
Explain the Chinese Room argument and evaluate the systems, robot and brain-substitute replies.
Identify which properties of modern benchmarks are Turing-test properties, and which are not: memorisation, style bias, judge limitations, contamination.

common_misconceptions: The Turing test is a test of intelligence - it is a test of indistinguishability from a human under a specific protocol, which is weaker and different.
The Chinese Room refutes AI: it targets a specific claim about symbolic computation and intentionality, and does not engage learning-based systems at all.
A Gödelian argument (Lucas/Penrose) shows humans outperform any machine; the standard reply is that it proves at most that no machine can prove its own consistency, which is a different fact.

topics.name: The Symbol-Grounding Problem and the Embodiment Hypotheses
topics.definition: Harnad's 1990 symbol-grounding problem: in a purely symbolic system, every symbol's meaning is defined only by further symbols, so the system can manipulate tokens indefinitely without ever touching the sensory world the tokens are supposed to be about. Grounding requires a mechanism by which some symbols acquire meaning non-symbolically.
topics.explanation: The argument is a refinement of Searle rather than a repetition of it: the issue is not intentionality as a metaphysical property but the semantics of a token system as a design problem. If the dictionary is the only source of definitions, learning words is circular. Harnad's proposed exit is robotic and categorical perception - a system that can discriminate sensorimotor features and is rewarded for doing so has some symbols grounded in magnitudes it can directly detect. The related family of theses, often conflated, is worth separating: (1) the embodiment thesis, that cognition depends on the body's sensorimotor system; (2) the situatedness thesis, that competence depends on real-time coupling to an environment, articulated by Brooks as intelligence without representation, i.e. that a sufficient controller can use the world as its own best model; (3) the extended-enactivist thesis, that cognition is constitutively embedded in social and material practice, argued by Winograd and Flores from Heidegger, with the distinction between present-at-hand readiness-to-hand and thematic representation as a critique of explicit-knowledge design; (4) the predictive/embodied-encoding thesis, that a representation is fit for an agent when its format matches the agent's action space, which is a design claim you can actually test. Empirically, the moderate form of embodiment has support and the strong form does not: camera and actuator geometry affect learned representations and control interfaces (visible in proprioceptive and visual-tactile encodings in manipulation); no experiment has shown that representation-free control scales to tasks that need deferred reasoning. The distributional-semantic critique, 'learning statistical distributional information about symbol use is not learning what symbols mean' (Bender and Koller's noun-staircase analysis), is the modern restatement of grounding for large language models, and it is a fair point about the mapping problem - it is a weaker point than its maximal rhetorical form because it does not establish that grounded symbol systems must be built the way GOFAI built them.

Brooks's claim was that no internal state is ever needed; his own robots, and subsumption architectures generally, maintain state.
Symbol grounding and the Chinese Room are the same argument; grounding is about the origin of meaning in a token system, Searle's is about sufficiency of syntax for intentionality.

topics.name: Levels of Description, the Cognitive Science Interface, and Benchmarks
topics.definition: Intelligence claims live at different descriptive levels - hardware/implementation, algorithmic representation, and goal-level 'why' - and most disputes arise from answering at one level while being asked at another. The field also inherits its evaluation culture from a specific, contested history of intelligence benchmarks.
topics.explanation: Marr's three levels (implementation, representation-and-algorithm, computational/why) are a working tool rather than a philosophy: they explain why 'the network does it by memorising' and 'the network does it by inferring the rule' can be true at different levels, and why an architecture question is not always evidence about a mechanism question. Dennett's intentional stance gives the complementary pragmatic rule: attribute beliefs and desires to a system only insofar as doing so yields reliable predictions, which is how we should read claims that a model 'knows' or 'plans'. The cognitive-science interface is where the field under-teaches most of its useful concepts: ACT-R and Soar formalise human knowledge structures as production and declarative systems; Bayesian cognitive science models human inductive inference as posterior inference over structured hypotheses, with sample-approximation accounts explaining human biases that look irrational under optimality-only framings; human learning data constrain what few-shot, compositional generalisation should even mean. The benchmark-politics layer is inseparable from all of this: IQ and psychometrics were designed by people with explicit agendas, and the practice of defining a single number for intelligence has always served classification more than understanding. In machine evaluation the same structural problems recur - an aggregate score hides distributional assumptions, datasets encode the priorities of whoever collected them, capability measures are contestable by construction, and 'general' benchmarks get retired as they saturate. The methodological answer is not to abandon benchmarks but to specify the task distribution, report capability against stated assumptions, keep failure modes visible, and separate diagnostic from ranking evaluations.

topics.name: Reading a Field's History Without Mythologising It
topics.definition: Historiography of AI is the practice of reconstructing what a field believed, on what evidence, and under what institutional incentives - while resisting the four standard distortions: founder memoir, hindsight narrative, paradigm propaganda, and the single-story teleology that ends in the present.
topics.explanation: Most published history of AI is written by participants with reputational stakes, and the failure modes are predictable. Founder memoir over-attributes paradigm shifts to insight rather than to funding, hardware and available data; the standard retelling of the 1956 Dartmouth workshop as the 'birth of AI' flattens the fact that the workshop was a modest research proposal with an aspirational one-page summary. Hindsight narrative presents the eventual winner as inevitable - so connectionism reads as having been 'the right answer' when in the 1960s it was one of several live programmes, and the perceptron controversy (Rosenblatt's claims against Minsky and Papert's 1969 limits result) is not a story of correctness but of a field's premature rejection of a learning paradigm that later returned with different mathematics. Paradigm propaganda is the tendency of each school to write the previous one as confused rather than as solving a different problem well: GOFAI was genuinely successful at tasks with a known symbolic structure, and its documented brittleness was in transfer and common sense, which the statistical paradigm solved only by changing the objective. Finally, teleology: the present foundation-model era is not the terminus implied by most current writing, and reading history forward rather than backwards is the discipline that prevents you treating today's methods as discovered rather than constructed. Practical method: prefer sources that quote contemporaneous claims with their dates; read critiques alongside the original (Lighthill as well as the 1965 seminar it responded to); distinguish an algorithm's invention from its successful deployment (backpropagation existed in multiple forms before 1986 and became useful only with data and compute); and treat a field's own success stories as its marketing. The same discipline applies to statistics and computing: check who funded the claim, what the metric was, and whether the reported result was reproducible at the time or only later reconstructed.

domains.name: Knowledge Representation and Automated Reasoning
domains.summary: The explicit-knowledge half of AI: formalisms for stating what is true, calculi for deriving what follows, solvers that make it computationally feasible, and the planning and verification layers built on top. This is the substrate under most reliable modern systems, including retrieval, guardrails, config validation and program synthesis.

subdomains.name: Representation Formalisms and Logic
subdomains.summary: From frames and semantic networks to description logics and ontologies, and from propositional/first-order calculi to the modal, epistemic and nonmonotonic logics needed by agents that reason about themselves, time, and incomplete knowledge.

topics.name: KR Formalisms: Frames, Semantic Networks, Description Logics, Ontologies
topics.definition: A knowledge-representation formalism is a language for stating facts and constraints about a domain together with an inference procedure whose guarantees you can name. Frames, semantic networks, conceptual graphs, ontologies and description logics are design points on a spectrum from expressive-but-intractable to tractable-but-thin.
topics.explanation: Minsky's frames (1975) and Schank and Abelson's scripts captured stereotyped situations as structures with default-filled slots and inheritance, solving the brittleness of naive logic for common-sense categories; the price was that defaults and inheritance interact badly, and the frame problem (which facts survive an action?) remained. Semantic networks (Ross Quillian's spreading activation for natural-language comprehension; later Sowa's conceptual graphs as a rigorous, isomorphic-to-logic version) made relations first-class and gave the retrieval metaphor that survives in today's embedding stores. Brachman's 1979 analysis of 'the notion of a representation for a reasoning system' is the key result: representation choice determines inference cost, so adding expressivity to a language can make inference undecidable or intractable even when the original task was easy - the reason Krypton and LOOM moved toward decidable fragments. Those fragments became description logics, the formal core of OWL and of every modern ontology: concepts, roles, individuals; TBox (terminological) and ABox (assertional) separation; reasoning tasks reduced to satisfiability, subsumption and instance checking with well-mapped worst-case complexities. The trade-off table is the practical content: propositional logic is cheap and cannot express structure; first-order logic is expressive and semi-decidable at best; DLS in the SROIQ family (OWL 2 DL) give NExpTime-complete reasoning with excellent practical reasoners; Datalog gives polynomial data complexity, which is why it, not full logic, runs at scale in industry. Ontologies at scale - SNOMED CT, Gene Ontology, Uberon, Wikidata, schema.org - teach the engineering lessons: ontology maintenance, versioning, and the distinction between a closed-world database and an open-world logic are harder than inference. Winograd and Flores's critique from Heidegger still applies to explicit-knowledge design: the more a system demands that users articulate in advance what they know, the more it will fail where knowledge is tacit.

topics.name: First-Order Logic and Automated Deduction
topics.definition: Automated deduction in first-order logic is the study of proof procedures - natural deduction, tableaux, resolution with unification - that derive consequences of a clause set mechanically, together with the fundamental negative result that no such procedure can be both complete and terminating for arbitrary first-order inputs.
topics.explanation: The engine is a small set of ideas. Unification solves for substitutions making two terms identical; it is decidable, has a most general unifier, and is the reason first-order inference can be goal-directed at all. Resolution, after conversion to clausal normal form, replaces a case analysis over interpretations with a single sound-and-complete rule on clauses; refutation completeness is what makes it work for proof by contradiction. Tableaux give the dual view - systematically expanding a formula to look for a closed branch - which is why DL reasoners use them: they support blocking arguments for decidability. Natural deduction (Gentzen/Prawitz style) matches human proof and underlies tactic-based interactive provers. Model elimination and connection-graph methods add structure-aware search. The theoretical limits matter as much as the algorithms: Church's 1936 result makes validity undecidable, so any theorem prover must either diverge or restrict the input; the decision problems for fragments (monadic, two-variable with counting, Bernays-Schoenfinkel) are the map for encoding a problem solvably. Ground reasoning is a design pattern worth learning: Skolemise, instantiate only the terms that appear in the goal, and hand the residual to a SAT solver - this is how most real 'first-order' verification works. Modern ATP systems (Vampire, E, Prover9) combine saturation with given-clause selection, deletion/discriminating-literal filtering, and learned literal preference; they win problems that humans find hard and lose problems a human solves instantly, which is the honest state of the art. Proof reconstruction and verification (checking a found proof in a trusted kernel) are what let ATP results enter certified pipelines.

topics.name: Modal, Epistemic and Temporal Logic for Agents
topics.definition: Modal logics add operators read as 'it is necessary/possible that' over accessibility relations between worlds. Instantiating those relations as time, knowledge, belief, obligation or action yields temporal logic (LTL/CTL), epistemic logic (S5, with common knowledge), deontic logic and dynamic epistemic logic - the standard formal languages for specifying what an agent or protocol is supposed to guarantee.
topics.explanation: The semantics is Kripke structures: a set of worlds, an accessibility relation per modality, a valuation. This single device makes otherwise-unrelated logics comparable and gives you completeness arguments against the right frame conditions - reflexivity and transitivity for knowledge (S4/S5), seriality for obligation, total order for linear time. Epistemic logic models what each agent knows (K_i phi), and the partition semantics over indistinguishability worlds explains why knowledge is factive while belief is not; Fagin, Halpern, Moses and Vardi's analysis made 'reasoning about knowledge' a resource- and complexity-question (model checking S5 is PSPACE-hard in the number of agents because accessibility is implicit in a state's local values). Common knowledge (everyone knows, everyone knows that everyone knows, ad infinitum) is the concept that separates ordinary distributed-systems reasoning from protocol correctness: the muddy-child and coordinated-attack problems show that achieving common knowledge over an asynchronous unreliable channel is impossible, which is the honest formal reason consensus protocols need timeouts, failure detectors or partial synchrony rather than cleverness. Temporal logic supplies the specification language for verification: LTL over paths with until/eventually operators, CTL with branching path quantifiers, and the LTL-to-Buchi-automaton construction with its safety/liveness hierarchy as the algorithmic core. Alternating-time temporal logic (ATL) quantifies over coalitions and gives strategic ability, which is the formal bridge to game theory and mechanism design. Dynamic epistemic logic models how announcements change knowledge, and its DEL semantics is essentially an announcement-update on Kripke models. The under-taught practical point is that these logics are the interface layer of reliability engineering: a robot's obligation to yield, a payment protocol's privacy property, and a multi-agent plan's deadlock-freeness all become modal formulas that a model checker can discharge.

topics.name: Nonmonotonic Reasoning: Defaults, Circumscription, Argumentation
topics.definition: Nonmonotonic logics let conclusions be withdrawn when new facts arrive: a system that infers 'birds fly' from 'Tweety is a bird' must be able to retract it upon learning 'Tweety is a penguin'. Monotonicity fails because classical consequence is closed under adding premises, and rational defeasible inference is not.
topics.explanation: Three formal families carry most of the content. Default logic (Reiter 1980) represents rules with justifications and requires a fixed point: the set of conclusions must equal what the defaults derive given those conclusions, giving extensions; normal defaults always have one, semi-normal defaults may have none, and the general case can have infinitely many. Autoepistemic logic (Moore 1985) reads the modal operator as 'I believe', so an agent reasons about its own beliefs and stability again is a fixed point; it is intertranslatable with default logic for a large fragment. Circumscription (McCarthy 1980) minimises the extension of predicates - 'assume the abnormality predicate is as small as possible' - and gives a second-order semantics that handles specificity ordering elegantly but is hard to compute. The computational facts are the sobering part: brave and sceptical consequence for propositional default logic are Sigma2^p and Pi2^p-complete respectively, one level above SAT, so practical systems compile to SAT with quantifier elimination or to answer-set programs. Argumentation frameworks (Dung 1995) replace rule semantics with a graph of arguments and an attack relation, and define acceptability through admissible, complete, preferred and stable extensions; their complexity table is the reason they are now a standard tool for explaining and adjudicating conflicts between rules, and they connect to ASP via the observed correspondence between stable extensions and stable models. Ranking-based systems (System Z, lexicative closure, conditional entropic inference) give a probabilistic reading of 'normally' with polynomial-time model checking for some fragments. The classic failure modes remain live and are exactly what a modern platform should teach: specificity conflicts, the Yale shooting problem (frame axioms and temporal persistence), and the multiplicity problem of many incomparable extensions.

topics.name: Logic Programming and Answer-Set Programming
topics.definition: Answer-set programming (ASP) is a style of declarative programming in which a program is a set of rules under stable-model semantics, its models are the admissible solutions to a problem, and a solver enumerates, optimises and explains them. Prolog is the operational relative, with negation-as-failure and unification but different semantics.
topics.explanation: Prolog's operational semantics is SLD-resolution with unification and backtracking, which is elegant and fast but does not implement the intended logical reading: a program can fail to derive a true consequence, and negation as failure means 'not provable' rather than 'false'. Adding constraints (CLP) or tabling fixes practical issues, not the semantics gap. Stable-model semantics (Gelfond & Lifschitz 1988) gives the fix for disjunction and classical negation: ground the program, remove rules whose negated bodies hit the candidate, take the least model of the remaining positive program, and require a fixed point. The result is a language where 'solve a puzzle by writing its rules' works. The software stack is what makes ASP teachable: lparse grounds, gluing/clever choice-point heuristics plus conflict-driven clause learning do the solving, and clingo is the modern system; aspif provides certificates. Encodings are a craft, and the design rules worth teaching explicitly: define a generate-and-test pattern with choice rules, write constraints not enumerations, use optimisation statements (#minimize) with stratification, exploit symmetry-breaking literals so the solver does not prove the same subproblem six times, and keep bounds tight for practicality. Datalog, the stratified fragment, is the workhorse for analytics: polynomial data complexity, engines embedded in SQL systems and property-graph databases, and the right language when recursion over large relations matters more than expressivity. Knowledge-representation reasoning tools built on ASP include diagnosis, configuration, and plan verification, where the ability to enumerate all solutions and to explain unsatisfiable cores is worth more than raw speed.

topics.name: SAT, SMT, and Constraint Solving
topics.definition: Boolean satisfiability and its extensions are the general-purpose engine of explicit reasoning: CDCL SAT solving decides propositional formulas, SMT adds theory solvers for arithmetic, bit-vectors, arrays and uninterpreted functions, and constraint programming adds global propagators over structured domains. Model counting (#SAT) turns the same machinery into a probability calculator.
topics.explanation: CDCL (conflict-driven clause learning) is a depth-first assignment search that, on conflict, analyses the implication graph to learn a clause that blocks a whole subtree, backtracks non-chronologically, and restarts periodically; its performance rests on three heuristics rather than on its completeness proof - VSIDS-style activity scores from conflict analysis, phase saving, and aggressive restart/larning schemes, plus watched-literal data structures that make unit propagation near-linear. Modern solvers add preprocessing (bounded variable elimination, subsumption, vivification), parallel portfolio and stochastic local-search phases, and proof logging (DRAT/LRAT) so results are auditable. SMT layers theory solvers over the same core with the Nelson-Oppen/EUF combination scheme, case-splitting for arithmetic, and lazy predicate abstraction; Z3, cvc5 and Bitwuzla are the systems, and their practical uses include bounded model checking, symbolic execution, configuration debugging and verifying that a compiler optimisation is safe. UNSAT cores and interpolation turn a solved instance into an explanation and into a reachable-state over-approximation; MaxSAT and its weighted variants handle soft constraints, which is where optimisation problems become solvable. #SAT and projected model counting are exact probabilistic inference once compiled into deterministic decomposable negation normal form (d-DNNF), giving the tractable-any-time route from logic to probability - #P-complete in theory, competitive on structured instances in practice. Constraint satisfaction brings a different algebra: arc and bounds consistency (AC-3 and its efficient successors), global constraints (AllDifferent, Cumulative, regular) with dedicated propagators, symmetry breaking, and local search (GSAT, walking, and the large-neighbourhood hybrid of LNS) for problems where propagation is too weak. The unifying engineering lesson across all four is that modelling is more important than solving: the same problem encoded with different variables can be six orders of magnitude apart in difficulty.

topics.name: Neuro-symbolic Methods, Program Synthesis, and ILP
topics.definition: Neuro-symbolic integration is the attempt to combine differentiable learning over distributed representations with symbolic reasoning over structured ones. Its concrete, working forms are program synthesis (search a space of programs consistent with examples), ILP (learn first-order rules from examples), and integration of a neural perception layer with a symbolic reasoner layer.
topics.explanation: Garcez and Lamb's 'third wave' framing states the design goal: a system that learns from data, reasons with explicit rules, and explains its conclusions, none of which today's architectures deliver together. The successful artefacts are narrower and instructive. Inductive logic programming learns logic programs from entailment: FOIL (Muggleton 1991) greedily specialises clauses to improve coverage/purity, and the modern lineage (Metagol, Popper) searches hypothesis spaces defined by metarules, with statistical-relevance and minimum-description-length criteria doing the pruning; ILP's attraction is interpretability plus compositionality. Version-space algebras (Mitchell 1978) and candidate-elimination remain the cleanest statement of the general problem and of its brittleness under noise. Inductive program synthesis (Solar-Lez?; the 'programming-by-examples' line) and inductive functional synthesis (Balog et al.'s Neural-Guided Deductive Search; Olya? Ellis et al.'s DreamCoder, which learns reusable library abstractions by stochastic recycling with a neural handout prior) show the two-directional flow: search gives the learner structure, and the learner gives search a prior. The perception-reasoning hybrids - NSC-VQA (Yi et al.), LEAPS, and DeepProbLog/ProbLog, where a neural module emits probabilistic facts consumed by a logic program with differentiable semantics - established the pattern of gradient training through a symbolic layer; semantic loss (Koh? Liang et al. NeurIPS 2018) generalises it by adding a differentiable penalty for logical validity instead of a full reasoner. Knowledge-base completion is where symbolic and statistical methods actually merge commercially: rule mining (AMIE, AnyBurl) plus embedding scoring, with the caveat that association-rule support does not imply causal validity. Retrieval-as-knowledge-representation is the pragmatic, widely deployed hybrid: an unstructured store plus an index becomes the external memory of a reasoning system, which is a position about where structure lives, not a solution to grounding. Honest limits: neuro-symbolic results are usually evaluated on synthetic compositional tasks; the 'explanation' produced is often a reconstruction rather than a causal account of the network; and no system yet demonstrates the combination at scale on open-domain data.

topics.name: Theorem Proving at Scale: ATPs, Interactive Provers, and AI-Assisted Mathematics
topics.definition: Two theorem-proving traditions now interact: automated provers (Vampire, E, Z3) that search for a refutation with no human guidance, and interactive provers (Coq, Isabelle/HOL, Lean) whose proofs are machine-checked in a small trusted kernel. AI-assisted mathematics attaches learning systems to the second tradition.
topics.explanation: The reason to care is the kernel. In an interactive prover a proof is accepted only if a tiny type-theoretic or higher-order logic checker verifies it, so the result is certified rather than merely plausible. Harrison's and de Moura's SAT/SMT-based automation of proof obligations showed that most 'trivial' steps in a big development are decidable-theory work, which is why SMT solvers sit under the tactic layer. ATPs contribute differently: given a problem translated to CNP/FOF (TPTP is the standard format and the CASC competition its benchmark), saturation-based provers now solve a large fraction of problems that humans pose, and their combination with an interactive prover (Sledgehammer in Isabelle, dp/LeanHammer in Lean) is the standard workflow: an ATP finds a candidate proof, the tactic replays it, the kernel accepts it. The frontier is the interesting part. AlphaProof (DeepMind, 2024) reached IMO-medallist level by learning to search Lean proof states with a value function trained on a synthetic problem generator and then using test-time compute to sample candidate proofs - the method is a search over formal states with a learned prior, and it is the cleanest demonstration of a capability that pure LLM text generation cannot provide. LeanDojo (Yang et al. 2023) made real Lean repositories into an environment for retrieval-augmented proof search, and ReProver plus equal-expression search (CoqGym) established that a learned retrieval over relevant premises beats earlier methods on premise selection, historically the biggest bottleneck. The honest limitations: auto-formalisation is the actual bottleneck (Tao's 'equational search for mathlib proofs' argument is that the labour is translation, not deduction); a proof assistant is only as good as its library; LLM-generated proofs produce many plausible-looking false candidates, so verifier-in-the-loop search rather than single-shot generation is mandatory; and the cost of writing the specification usually exceeds the cost of writing the code. Beyond mathematics the same machinery is used for verified compilation (CompCert), and for runtime verification where a finite trace is checked against an LTL property - cheaper and more scalable than exhaustive model checking.

topics.name: Search Algorithms, Heuristics, and Classical Planning
topics.definition: Search is the substrate: A* with an admissible heuristic is the canonical optimal algorithm, and classical planning is its most developed application - describe a state space in PDDL, estimate distance with a relaxed-problem heuristic, and search forward, backward, or in a partial order.
topics.explanation: Breadth-first and depth-first search trade memory for optimality; iterative deepening (Korf 1985) recovers optimality at linear space and is nearly free with unit costs. A* (Hart, Nilsson & Raphael 1968) is optimal for a given heuristic iff the heuristic is admissible, and its efficiency is governed by how closely h approximates true cost; weighted A* trades a bounded suboptimality factor for speed and dominates practical use; bidirectional search halves depth; anytime variants (ARA*, anytime weighted A*, RRT*-style replanning) deliver a solution now and improve it later, which is what robotics needs. Beam search is the greedy approximation - cheap, not optimal, and the reason sequence models generate multiple candidates. Local search (hill climbing, GSAT/WalkSAT for SAT, simulated annealing, tabu) attacks problems where a path is unnecessary, and anytime local search with restarts is the pragmatic industrial answer. Adversarial search covers minimax with alpha-beta pruning, whose pruning efficiency is entirely about move ordering (and transposition tables in practice), and expectiminimax plus MCTS/UCT, where the rollout value estimate plus the UCB exploration bonus gives regret-bounded selection; AlphaZero replaced handcrafted evaluation with a policy/value network and self-play, which is the modern synthesis of search and learning. Planning formalises the whole thing. STRIPS (Fikes & Nilsson 1971) supplies the preconditions/add/delete model; PDDL is its standard syntax and defines domains and problems, with derived predicates, durative actions and hierarchical extensions as the important variants. GraphPlan (Blum & Furst 1995) introduced the planning graph with mutual exclusion and the idea that a reachability structure can yield both an admissible heuristic (set-level and, via relaxed-problem reachability, h_max) and a solution extractor. Heuristic-search planners (HSP, LPG, FastDownward's landmark-count and causal-graph heuristics, LAMA's focus search) turned admissible heuristic construction into an automatic procedure over any PDDL domain; optimal planning is now practical for moderate problems via downward-cumulative costs. The lesson that does not get taught: the state space is what you declare, so modelling choices (variable granularity, derived fluents, action abstraction) determine solvability more than the solver does.

topics.name: Planning under Uncertainty, Partial Observability, and Temporal Domains
topics.definition: Real planning problems have incompletely specified initial state, stochastic or unknown effects, time windows, and other agents. The formal answers are contingent and conformant planning, hierarchical task networks, temporal and multi-agent planning, partially observable Markov decision processes, and task-and-motion planning that couples symbolic goals to geometric feasibility.
topics.explanation: Start with the classical assumption you are dropping: full observability and determinism. Conformant planning produces a single plan guaranteed to work for every initial state in a belief set - sound but often infeasible. Contingent planning emits a policy: a branch structure with observations as conditions, guaranteed to reach the goal for every admissible outcome; the standard algorithm is regression plus AND-OR search (Cimatti et al.'s CONP/Min-Conf), and its scaling is poor because the policy is exponential in the number of observations. Probabilistic temporal planning (PPTL/TEMPLO, RPNP) adds duration and chance; POMDPs (Kaelbling, Littman & Cassandra 1998) are the general stochastic-partial framework, with exact value iteration over belief space infeasible and practical solutions being point-based backup (PBVI, HIVM, SARSOP's bounds) or online rollout (POMCP, and its successors using particle belief representations). The crucial conceptual point is the belief-state MDP: planning is done in a continuous belief simplex even when the underlying state space is finite, which is why learning a good belief representation is a modelling problem. Hierarchical task network planning (HTN; NOAH through SHOP2) handles 'what to do' by decomposing compound tasks with methods, and its practical significance is that abstraction can be sound or unsound depending on whether the decomposition preserves goal reachability - a theorem-level question. Multi-agent planning adds coordination, decomposing a joint goal into subgoals with ordering and resource constraints (partial-order planning with concurrency), and its hard cases are symmetric conflict resolution and negotiation cost. Task-and-motion planning (TAMP) is the robotics coupling: a symbolic planner proposes action sequences whose parameters live in a continuous configuration space, and a motion planner must certify feasibility; the design space is whether the coupling is deferred (and re-planned on failure - the classic loose coupling) or tight (optimise jointly via nonlinear programming or MILP with big-M encoding of disjunctive constraints). The state of the art in all of these is 'search plus learned proposal': a learned prior over actions, subgoals or branch points, with symbolic machinery doing the guaranteeing. The under-taught caveat is identifiability of the model itself: a planner is only as good as the action-model completeness, and action-model acquisition is an open problem.

topics.name: Expert Systems, Rule Engines, and Retrieval as Knowledge Representation
topics.definition: Expert systems encoded domain knowledge as rules plus an inference engine and got the engineering lessons - knowledge acquisition bottleneck, maintenance, explanation, uncertainty - that recur wherever a system must be auditable. Their modern descendants are rule engines, guardrail policy systems, and retrieval-augmented architectures that externalise knowledge into a store.
topics.explanation: The historical arc is instructive rather than quaint. Dendral (Feigenbaum, Buchanan, Lederberg 1971) demonstrated that a weak search method plus a strong domain knowledge base could do plausible scientific hypothesis generation for mass spectra. MYCIN (Shortliffe) introduced certainty factors, an ad hoc Bayesian-looking calculus for combining evidence, and showed that explanation facilities ('why' and 'how' traces) were the acceptance-critical feature in clinical use. XCON/R1 (McDermott 1982) configured VAX orders and saved DEC tens of millions of dollars annually, proving the commercial case, and then proved the failure case too: it required constant hand maintenance and could not adapt. The engineering findings from this literature generalise. First, knowledge acquisition is the bottleneck, because experts cannot verbalise their heuristics; the standard remedy was a knowledge engineer as interpreter, which is why today's LLM-based elicitation experiments are genuinely new. Second, rule sets are brittle under distribution shift: an exception you did not write down is a wrong answer with full confidence. Third, uncertainty combination rules that are not probability are dangerous, exactly as Shaf?/Chand? critiques established - the certainty-factor calculus is not coherent, and the field learned that lesson twice (once with MYCIN, once with fuzzy logic in control). Fourth, explanation is a user-interface requirement, not a by-product of symbolic machinery, and the tracing machinery (TMS, justification-based networks) is directly relevant to today's need to say why a policy blocked an action. Fifth, verification and validation of knowledge bases is a research area in itself: redundancy, conflict, and completeness checking of rule sets reduces to SAT/ASP problems. The modern descendants keep parts: forward-chaining production systems survive as Rete-algorithm rule engines in fraud, networking and configuration; ontologies plus logic survive in biomedical data integration; and retrieval-as-knowledge-representation (RAG, semantic memory over vector stores) is a bet that an unstructured store plus a similarity index can substitute for an explicit logic - the honest assessment is that it delivers coverage and cheap updates but loses consistency checking, contradiction detection, and guaranteed entailment. The correct comparison is not 'rules versus retrieval' but which parts of a task need guarantees and which need coverage.

topics.name: Bayesian Modelling and Inference in Practice
topics.definition: Bayesian inference is the disciplined computation of a posterior distribution p(theta | y) proportional to likelihood times prior. In practice it is a modelling engineering problem: choose a parameterisation and factorisation that makes the posterior tractable, compute the quantities you actually need (predictive distributions, not parameters), compare models by marginal likelihood, and check that the whole thing reproduces data.
topics.explanation: The analytic core is worth having at your fingertips: exponential families are the family of likelihoods with sufficient statistics and conjugate priors, so a Gaussian with known variance, a binomial, a Poisson, a multinomial-Dirichlet and a normal-gamma model each admit closed-form posteriors, and posterior updating is then statistics, not calculus. Conjugacy exists because the natural parameter is linear in the sufficient statistic; when you leave the exponential family or add latent structure, you lose it and buy an approximation algorithm instead. Hierarchical (multilevel) models place priors on the parameters of group-level effects, and partial pooling is their defining and most useful property: a small-sample group's estimate is shrunk toward the population mean, which is both better prediction and a better explanation of why naive per-group estimates mislead. Nonparametric extensions replace a finite parameter vector with a distribution over structures - Dirichlet processes for mixture orders, Gaussian processes for functions, Indian-buffer/CRP constructions for latent features - where the 'number of parameters' grows with data under a prior that puts mass on all sizes. Probabilistic programming languages separate model from inference engine: Stan (Hamiltonian Monte Carlo plus Laplace and variational options) targets static continuous models; Pyro and WebPPL/Gen support discrete latent variables, data subsampling and custom inference, with Gen making the inference algorithm itself programmable (simulation, importance, MCMC kernels over the same model); Church pioneered the higher-order generative-program view. The two practices that separate competent Bayesians from cargo-cult users are posterior predictive checking (simulate replicated datasets and look for systematic disagreement) and computing the marginal likelihood p(y) for model comparison - hard because it is an integral over a region that the prior explored only rarely, which is why bridge sampling, importance sampling, thermodynamic integration and Laplace approximations exist. The model-selection ladder, from AIC/BIC (asymptotic, likelihood-based) through Bayes factors (exact but prior-sensitive, with the Lindley-Bartlett and Jeffreys-Lindley paradoxes as warnings) to minimum description length (coding-length as complexity), is a set of approximations to the same quantity with different failure modes.

topics.name: Graphical Models: Representation, Inference, and Structure Learning
topics.definition: A probabilistic graphical model uses a graph to record which random variables are conditionally independent of which others, turning a joint distribution into a product of local factors whose size is exponential only in the graph's connectivity rather than in the number of variables.
topics.explanation: Directed Bayesian networks factorise as the product of conditional probability tables, and their independence semantics are d-separation; undirected Markov random fields factorise over cliques of an undirected graph, with conditional independence read from graph separation and, by the Hammersley-Clifford theorem, log-linear structure over clique potentials. Junction-tree (clique-tree) compilation converts either into a tree over clusters and makes exact inference linear in cluster size - the cost reappearing as treewidth, which is the fundamental hardness measure for the whole field. Factor graphs add explicit nodes for every factor and unify sum-product and max-product under one message-passing rule; they are the natural language of coding theory, of SLAM, and of inference engines with reusable factors. Learning splits into parameter learning (complete data gives decoupled maximum-likelihood per conditional; missing latent structure requires EM or gradient through a relaxed representation) and structure learning, which is where the real difficulty lives. Score-based search maximises BIC, BDeu or a cross-validated likelihood over a DAG space that is super-exponential, using hill climbing with edge additions/deletions/reversals and acyclicity handled by ancestry checks or by continuous reformulations; Chickering's equivalence-class search is the principled version, since Markov-equivalent DAGs (same skeleton, same v-structures) are indistinguishable from observational data. Constraint-based methods test conditional independencies and orient what remains (PC and its ancestral SGS), and FCI extends this to latent confounders by returning a partial ancestral graph rather than a DAG. The hybrid and modern differentiable branches (GES ordering search, NOTEARS-style continuous acyclicity constraints) are treated in the causal-learning topic because their target is a causal graph, not a Markov equivalence class. Markov logic networks and probabilistic soft logic show the log-linear model meeting first-order logic - weighted formulas as features, with a soft ground predicate in [0,1] - which is the standard representation for relational probabilistic inference and the reason statistical and symbolic AI are not opposites. Practical wisdom: graphical models are a poor fit for high-dimensional perception and a superb fit for structured decisions with modest state spaces, and the modern use is hybrid - a neural net producing the parameters of a graphical model's factors.

topics.name: Approximate Inference: Loopy BP, Variational Methods, EP, and AMP
topics.definition: When exact inference is #P-hard or the factors are non-conjugate, approximate inference replaces the true posterior with a tractable one. The three governing principles are fixed-point message passing, divergence minimisation over a restricted family, and moment/energy matching on local exponential families.
topics.explanation: Loopy belief propagation runs sum-product on a graph with cycles and iterates messages to a fixed point. Its status is unusual and worth understanding precisely: exact on trees, it typically gives good answers on graphs with weak local cycles, and its failure modes are strong loops and oscillation; its fixed points correspond to stationary points of the Bethe free energy, which is the bridge to variational thinking, and damping or a mini-cluster schedule can rescue convergence. Mean-field variational inference restricts the posterior to a fully factorised family and minimises forward/reverse KL by coordinate updates; its weakness is underestimating variance and its strength is speed and scalability to stochastic optimisation, which is why the reparameterisation/score-gradient versions (black-box VI) power large-scale latent-variable models. A key conceptual point that is often fumbled: variational autoencoders are amortised variational inference on a graphical model, not a separate technology. Expectation propagation (Minka 2001) is the third member and the most practically useful for non-conjugacy: it maintains local exponential-family approximations to individual factors and updates each by moment matching of the tilted distribution, which yields Gaussian-process and robust-regression inference at a cost comparable to mean-field but with better variance estimates; assumed-density filtering is its sequential cousin. Generalised expectation propagation and mixture EP handle discrete and multimodal factors. Approximate message passing comes from statistical physics rather than machine learning: on dense, random-like instances its fixed points coincide with the sum-product equations, and its state-evolution recursion characterises when it is optimal - the source of the replica-method results in compressed sensing, sparse regression, spin glasses and the analysis of SGD. In practice the ranking is: try a compiled exact method if treewidth permits; use HMC for low-dimensional continuous posteriors; use EP for conjugate-ish structured models; use VI for scale; use AMP only when its structural assumptions hold.

topics.name: Monte Carlo, MCMC, and Sequential Monte Carlo in Practice
topics.definition: Sampling-based inference estimates intractable integrals by drawing from, or simulating trajectories into, a target distribution: plain Monte Carlo and importance sampling when you can reach the target directly, MCMC when you can only evaluate an unnormalised density, and sequential Monte Carlo when the target is a filtering distribution you can only reach step by step.
topics.explanation: Plain Monte Carlo's error is O(1/sqrt(N)) regardless of dimension, which is its entire selling point and also the reason the rest of this topic exists: it needs an easy proposal that covers the target. Importance sampling fixes the proposal mismatch but its weights degenerate in high dimension (effective sample size collapses), which is why self-normalised importance sampling is used for evidence estimates rather than posterior samples, and why nested sampling and the sequential variants exist. Rejection sampling is exact, unbiased, and only viable in low dimension with a bounded envelope. MCMC replaces independent draws with a reversible Markov chain whose stationary distribution is the target: Metropolis-Hastings with a Gaussian random-walk proposal is universal but slow and step-size-critical, with the optimal scaling result giving a target acceptance rate of roughly 0.234 in high dimension; Gibbs sampling exploits full conditionals and is unbeatable for discrete or conjugate models but stalls under near-deterministic dependence; slice sampling is tuning-light and robust; Hamiltonian Monte Carlo embeds the negative log-density in a mechanical system and uses the gradient to move along the contours rather than random-walking, with NUTS removing the trajectory-length parameter and the practical pipeline being warmup (mass-matrix/dual-tree adaptation) followed by divergence-and-treedepth diagnostics. Convergence checking is a craft: R-hat across chains, effective sample size per second rather than per draw, autocorrelation, and divergent-transition counts as an indicator of geometric pathology, not a nuisance. Parallel tempering runs chains at several inverse temperatures with swaps to escape local modes, and is the right answer for genuinely multimodal posteriors. Sequential Monte Carlo propagates a weighted particle set through a state-space model, resampling when weight degeneracy appears; the bootstrap filter, the optimal proposal, and auxiliary particle filters trade cost against particle diversity, and SMC is the standard nonlinear non-Gaussian estimator in robotics. Approximate Bayesian Computation drops the likelihood entirely and accepts parameter values whose simulated summaries are close to observed summaries - unbiased when the statistic is sufficient, otherwise trading bias for feasibility, with sequential Monte Carlo-ABC and neural-summary approaches controlling the damage.

topics.name: Gaussian Processes as a Modelling Framework
topics.definition: A Gaussian process specifies a distribution over functions such that every finite collection of function values is multivariate Gaussian, fully determined by a mean function and a covariance (kernel) function. Conditioning on data gives the posterior predictive mean and variance in closed form.
topics.explanation: The kernel is the model. Its choice encodes which function shapes are a priori plausible: the squared-exponential kernel gives infinitely differentiable sample paths and a characteristic length scale; Matern kernels trade smoothness for realism; periodic and spectral-mixture kernels encode cycles; linear and polynomial kernels encode global trends; and composition rules (sums for independent additive structure, products for shared multiplicative structure) let you build a model that reflects a mechanism rather than a curve. This makes GP regression an interpretable, Bayesian alternative to deep networks on small-to-medium data, with an honest predictive variance - the reason it dominates expensive-black-box optimisation, spatial statistics (kriging is GP regression), and low-data engineering models. The cost is the O(n^3) Cholesky factorisation and O(n^2) storage, which is why the scalable-GP literature is a field of its own: sparse approximations place M inducing points and approximate the posterior with a conditional-Gaussian low-rank structure (FITC, and the fully-correct predictive variance of DTC/TIC), the variational sparse GP of Titsias (2009) optimises a KL bound that avoids the double-counting of noise in earlier schemes, Hensman's stochastic gradient variational approach scales to millions of points, and structured approaches (grid/kernel-hierarchical interpolation, KISS-GP, circulant embedding, local-approximation schemes like LOTUS/LOKI) exploit stationarity or geometry. Hyperparameter learning is marginal-likelihood maximisation, typically with gradients, and its pathologies (length scales running to the prior boundary, non-identifiability of noise and length-scale combinations) are the practical difficulty most users meet. GP classification is intractable exactly and handled by EP or Laplace or a probit/mixture approximation; the label likelihood plus kernel plus latent function is the model. Two further uses define the modern GP agenda: multi-output and deep GPs (compositions of GPs as architectures) and the GP as the model class over which Bayesian optimisation acquires. The honest limits are the smoothness/stationarity assumptions, the Gaussian-likelihood bias on heavy-tailed data, and that O(n) inducing-point dimensionality, not kernel expressivity, caps what the model can say.

topics.name: Bayesian Optimization and Bayesian Experimental Design
topics.definition: Sequential decision-making under an expensive objective: Bayesian optimisation maximises a black-box function by repeatedly fitting a probabilistic surrogate (usually a GP) and choosing the next query point with an acquisition function that prices exploration; Bayesian experimental design chooses experiments before seeing any data to maximise information about parameters.
topics.explanation: The core is a loop: surrogate, uncertainty, a criterion that trades expected improvement against uncertainty, and re-fitting. Common acquisition functions and their actual behaviour: probability of improvement (greedy, weak exploration), expected improvement (EI, the default), upper/lower confidence bound (UCB, with the exploration parameter kappa giving an anytime regret-flavoured control), and knowledge-gradient/entropy-search, which evaluate the expected information gain about the maximiser rather than the expected function gain. The theory lives in the bandit literature: GP-UCB regret bounds show sublinear regret under a kernel-complexity measure that links the kernel's eigenvalue decay to hardness, which is the formal reason smooth problems with fast spectral decay are solved efficiently; finite-armed UCB and Thompson sampling give the discrete analogue, with Thompson's 1933 heuristic recently proven to have strong regret guarantees in several settings. Practical failures are as instructive as the theory: dimensionality above roughly 10-30 breaks the kernel's concentration advantage (remedies are random-embedding/REMbo/SAASBO, trust-region methods like TuRBO, and additive structure), parallel batches need the counterfactual trick or a qEI approximation, constraints require either feasibility-weighted EI or a separate classifier, non-stationarity and drift need sliding windows or change detection, and hyperparameter estimation noise can dominate the acquisition. Bayesian experimental design is the same logic applied before any observation: maximise expected information gain (the mutual information between design outcomes and parameters, e.g. D-optimality as expected log-determinant of the information matrix), or minimise a decision-theoretic risk; the computation is a nested expectation, approximated by variational bounds (variational information gain, BALD, AMIGO) or by MC with a learned posterior. The classic applications are optimal sensor placement, dose-finding, and the choice of informative next stimulus in psychophysics; the modern application is active learning and self-driving laboratories.

topics.name: Uncertainty Quantification, Calibration, and Conformal Prediction
topics.definition: Uncertainty quantification asks, for a trained predictor, how large its errors will be and whether its stated confidence matches its realised accuracy. Decomposition into epistemic (model/knowledge, reducible with data) and aleatoric (intrinsic noise, irreducible) uncertainty plus distribution-free coverage guarantees are the two modern pillars.
topics.explanation: Calibration for a classifier means that among instances predicted with probability p, the empirical success rate is p; the practical estimators are reliability diagrams (binned accuracy versus mean confidence), expected calibration error, and maximum calibration error. Modern neural networks are systematically overconfident (Guo et al. 2017), and the remedies form a hierarchy: temperature scaling (one parameter, works well, post-hoc), vector/matrix scaling, and non-parameterised binning methods such as histogram or isotonic recalibration; multiclass calibration needs class-wise treatment (dirichlet calibration) or vector scaling, and group-conditional calibration (calibration within demographic or task groups) is the fairness-relevant version, which is strictly harder than marginal calibration. For regressors, calibration means predictive-interval coverage and the distributional form, which is where conformal prediction is the genuinely important idea: given a nonconformity score and a calibration set, the split-conformal interval has exact finite-sample marginal coverage 1-alpha with no distributional assumption, using only exchangeability; quantile regression with conformalised scores gives adaptive width (CQR); conformalised prediction (Lei et al.) covers classification with set-valued predictions; and extensions handle covariate shift (weighted conformal), sequential validity (online conformal / ACI), and the group-conditional impossibility results, which state that exact conditional coverage cannot be achieved without strong assumptions - so you must choose which marginal or which group guarantee matters. Epistemic versus aleatoric: heteroscedastic likelihoods model input-dependent noise, ensembles and Monte-Carlo dropout model model-uncertainty, and the Kendall-Gal decomposition is a modelling choice that is not exactly identifiable (a mixture of two uncertainty sources is generally not separable without assumptions). Bayesian deep learning in practice: MC-dropout is an approximate variational inference in a Bayesian net, and its limits are now well documented (it under-disperses, dropout noise is not a posterior sample in general, and it does not capture weight-space geometry); deep ensembles empirically outperform nearly every posterior-approximation method at far lower conceptual cost; last-layer Laplace (Laplace-Last and the KL-regularised variants) gives a cheap, principled posterior with better calibration than dropout and is currently the pragmatic default for fine-tuned models. Selective prediction and abstention close the loop to decisions: risk-coverage curves, conformal risk control, and the 'say nothing' option. The right message to teach is that a prediction without an uncertainty statement is not a completed model.

domains.name: Causal Inference and Causal AI
domains.summary: The mathematics of what would happen if you intervened, rather than what is associated. Two formal traditions (potential outcomes and structural causal models), the identification questions that determine whether an answer is possible at all, and the places where causal reasoning changes machine learning practice.

subdomains.name: Causal Formalisms and Identification
subdomains.summary: Potential outcomes versus structural causal models, graphical semantics, do-calculus, and the identifiability questions that decide whether data can answer a causal query.

topics.name: Correlation, Causation, and the Two Formalisms
topics.definition: A causal effect compares outcomes across worlds that differ only in a treatment. The potential-outcomes (Rubin-Neyman) formalism writes this as a contrast between the values a unit would take under each treatment; the structural-causal-model (Pearl) formalism writes it as the distribution induced by an intervention on a set of equations. Both make precise why predictive accuracy is not evidence about intervention.
topics.explanation: The central obstacle is the fundamental problem of causal inference: a unit is observed under one treatment only, so individual effects are never observed, and every method is a strategy for constructing the missing half. Potential outcomes define the estimand first (ATE, ATT, conditional effects) and treat identification as a property of assumptions: consistency/SUTVA (one version of treatment, no interference between units), ignorability / conditional exchangeability (treatment assignment is as good as random given measured covariates), and positivity (every unit has nonzero probability of every treatment). In a DAG, ignorability is the backdoor criterion, and Pearl's do-calculus - three rules over interventions, observations and their combination - decides whether any interventional query is estimable from observational data plus a graph, which is a decision procedure rather than folklore. Structural causal models add machinery potential outcomes lack: explicit causal mechanisms, counterfactuals as compositions of abduction-action-prediction on a solved model, mediation, transportability across populations, and a language for 'given what actually happened, what would have happened otherwise'. The distinction that matters pedagogically is that a prediction model answers 'what is this associated with' while an intervention answers 'what changes if I set X'; in a graph with confounding, or where the training distribution was itself shaped by selection on the outcome, a high-accuracy model can be an arbitrarily bad guide to action - the classic case being the 'sicker patients get treated, so treatment looks harmful' inversion. Modern machine learning needs this because the failure modes are the common ones: off-policy evaluation in a recommender confounded by a ranker, fairness measured on a biased label, distribution shift because the covariate-outcome relation is stable only under the mechanism you did not change, and language models trained on data generated by earlier model outputs. A further subtlety worth teaching early: causality is a property of a generative mechanism, so the estimand, the identifying assumption, and the empirical strategy must be aligned from the start; a causal claim cannot be salvaged by better estimation.

topics.name: Structural Causal Models, Interventions, and Counterfactuals
topics.definition: A structural causal model is a set of assignments V_i = f_i(pa_i, U_i) over endogenous and exogenous variables, inducing a DAG, an observational distribution, an interventional distribution for every intervention, and - given a realised outcome - a counterfactual distribution over what would otherwise have happened.
topics.explanation: The ladder is the organising idea: rung 1 associations P(Y|X), rung 2 interventions P(Y | do(X)), rung 3 counterfactuals P(Y_x | X = x', Y = y'). An SCM with independently distributed exogenous noise is the standard assumption that makes rung 3 computable, and the algorithm is abduction (posterior on U given evidence), action (replace the equation for the intervened variable), prediction (solve the modified model). Graphs beyond DAGs matter once latent variables are present: MAGs (maximal ancestral graphs) represent the marginal distribution over observed variables with latent confounders and selection, and PAGs (partial ancestral graphs) encode what causal-discovery can certify from a MAG, with bidirected and undirected edges standing for 'some unmeasured cause' and 'orientation undetermined'. The do-calculus rules (insertion/deletion of actions, action/observation exchange, insertion/deletion of observations) are the syntactic counterpart of graph surgery and, in the DAG case, sound and complete (Huang & Valtorta; Shpitser & Pearl), with a polynomial algorithm (ID) computing interventional effects by backdoor split, and the more general identification procedure for arbitrary queries being complete for the nonparametric model. Mediation analysis asks how much of an effect flows through a specified path: natural direct and indirect effects (Pearl 2001, Robins & Greenland 1992) are counterfactual quantities and are identifiable only under strong cross-world independence assumptions, which is the technical content behind the common-sense warning that 'mediation' analysis is fragile. Transportability extends the whole apparatus across populations: reweighting by a selection mechanism decides when an effect estimated in one environment transfers, with invariance-based and conditional-transferability results as the machine-learning-facing versions. The practical value for an ML engineer is conceptual hygiene: most 'causal ML' claims that cannot name the graph, the intervention and the estimand do not survive review.

topics.name: Causal Discovery: Algorithms, Assumptions, and the Limits of Identifiability
topics.definition: Causal discovery is learning a causal graph from data without experimental intervention. Its guarantees come in two grades: learning an equivalence class under purely observational Gaussian/nonparametric assumptions, and learning a full orientation only when an additional distributional asymmetry (non-Gaussianity, additive-noise independence, or a known intervention locus) is exploited.
topics.explanation: The constraint-based line, PC and its stable variant, tests conditional independencies from data and returns a CPDAG - the Markov equivalence class, in which v-structures and colliders are oriented but remaining edges are undirected, because observational independence cannot distinguish X->Y from Y->X once no other variable is involved. FCI extends this when latent confounders or selection are possible and returns a PAG, which is the honest output in most observational settings. Score-based methods (GES, and Chickering's PCC algorithm on equivalence classes) optimise BIC/BDeu and are more robust to test error, which is why practical systems prefer them; LiNGAM exploits a linear-plus-non-Gaussian model to identify the full DAG, with pairwise likelihood-ratio measures (Hyvarinen & Smith) and DirectLiNGAM as the practical algorithms, and the result that orientation is identifiable there is the sharpest 'extra assumption buys identifiability' theorem in the field. The continuous-optimisation line (NOTEARS and its successors, DAG-GNN, and the acyclicity-constraint family) recasts structure learning as a smooth constrained problem, giving scalability but inheriting the parametric model's assumptions; recent work has shown the resulting linear-program/penalty formulations can be solved more stably. Granger causality is a time-series notion - predictability improvement from a past - and is neither necessary nor sufficient for causal influence, which is why PCMCI and PCMCI+ (Runge) combine a conditional-independence screen with time-lagged PC search and report effect sizes with p-values controlled under autocorrelation. The sober limits must be taught explicitly: with only observational data and a fully connected latent model, identifiability can be nil; a graph over variables you chose is a claim about those variables' granularity; conditional independence test power collapses with high-dimensional conditioning sets; faithfulness violations (parameter cancellation) break the guarantees; and the equivalence class is the strongest honest statement for the Gaussian-linear case. Causal discovery remains the weakest link between causal theory and application, and the correct posture is 'propose orientations, then test them with a designed intervention'.

topics.name: Treatment-Effect Estimation with Machine Learning
topics.definition: Estimating causal effects when confounders are high-dimensional: nuisance functions (propensity score and outcome regression) are learned by flexible ML, and the estimator is constructed so that first-order errors in those nuisances cancel (double/debiased machine learning), after which heterogeneity in the effect can be modelled.
topics.explanation: The estimands: ATE, ATT, and the conditional average treatment effect (CATE) tau(x) = E[Y(1)-Y(0) | X=x], which is the target for individualised decisions. The classic adjustment is the g-formula/regression adjustment and its inverse-probability-weighting cousin, with the propensity-score result (Rosenbaum & Rubin) that balancing on a scalar score under ignorability suffices, and the stabilised/trimmed-weight and overlap diagnostic (histograms of estimated propensity) as the practical check. Doubly robust/AIPW estimators combine both: the influence-function-based estimator remains consistent if either nuisance is correct and attains the semiparametric efficiency bound when both are, and its cross-fitting (split-sample nuisance fitting) is what removes overfitting bias from flexible ML nuisances - the honest statement of why modern causal ML works. Meta-learners (S/T/X-learner, R-learner, DR-learner) are CATE estimators differing in which residualisation they use; the R-learner's Robinson decomposition and the DR-learner's pseudo-outcome regression are the two principled constructions, with the latter inheriting the double-robustness. Causal forests and honest tree ensembles estimate tau(x) with local-averaging plus inference-valid confidence intervals; uplift modelling is the marketing-facing version, with the Qini/AUUC curve as the metric. The failure modes are the teaching content: positivity violations (a region where treatment was never assigned, where extrapolation is invention), weak instruments and near-deterministic assignment, extreme weights, effect heterogeneity confounded with propensity ('propensity score and treatment effect are jointly modelled by one flexible learner unless deliberately separated'), and the fact that a well-estimated CATE on a confounded observational dataset is not automatically transportable to a new site. Off-policy evaluation in recommendation is the same problem with logging propensity as the instrument - inverse-propensity, doubly robust, and self-normalised estimators trade variance against bias under overlap failure.
